title: Matthew (21 September)
hook: a tax collector at his table hears two words and gets up

segments.voice: Yesterday, Andrew Kim Taegon and his companions. Your line was korea's martyrs. Did you hold Korea in mind for a moment? Day one thousand twenty-seven.

A table by the road, coins stacked on it, a ledger open. The man behind it collects taxes, and in the gospels his trade is named in the same breath as sinners. Nobody stops to chat. Then someone does stop. He looks at the man at the table and says two words. Follow me. The gospel doesn't record a speech, a debate, a night to think it over. It records a man standing up. Today, Matthew.
screen: `A TABLE BY THE ROAD.` → `TWO WORDS: FOLLOW ME.` → `A MAN STANDS UP.`

segments.voice: The whole call takes one verse. In the Douay-Rheims, Jesus sees a man sitting in the custom house, named Matthew, and says to him: "Follow me. And he arose up and followed him." That's it. Mark and Luke tell the same scene and call the man Levi; Catholic tradition reads Levi and Matthew as one person. Now look at what he left. Some readers point to a difference: a fisherman like Peter could go back to his boats, and in John's gospel he does. A man who walked away from a tax post, those readers say, had no boat to go back to. And what does he do first? Luke says he made Jesus a great feast in his own house. Matthew's gospel says Jesus sat at table in the house, and many publicans and sinners came and sat down with him. Some onlookers asked his disciples why their teacher ate with such people. Jesus answered with a doctor's logic: "They that are in health need not a physician, but they that are ill." Then he sent them to a line from the prophet Hosea: "I will have mercy and not sacrifice." So the first thing a newly called man did was invite his old crowd to meet the one who called him. He didn't hide where he came from. The book that opens the New Testament carries his name, and Catholic tradition holds him to be its author. In that gospel, the man is named plainly: Matthew the publican. He kept the old label right next to the new life.
screen: `ONE VERSE: FOLLOW ME, AND HE AROSE.` · `SOME SAY: NO BOAT TO GO BACK TO.` · `HIS FIRST ACT: A DINNER FOR HIS CROWD.` · `HE KEPT THE NAME: MATTHEW THE PUBLICAN.` · then, large: `I WILL HAVE MERCY AND NOT SACRIFICE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: leave one thing to follow. Sit back and let your breathing slow. Notice what's on your table right now, the thing you keep checking, the stack you keep counting. It might be your phone, a worry, a grudge. Choose one, and for these two minutes, set it down. Literally, if you can: turn the phone over, close the tab. If you pray, you can hear the two words, follow me, and simply stay with them. If you don't, notice what it feels like to stand up from something. The bell holds the time.
Matthew. The tax collector who heard two words, got up from his table, and then threw a dinner so his old friends could meet the man who called him.
Your line: he arose and followed. Today, when you catch yourself stuck at the same table, stand up once, on purpose, and go toward something better. Day one thousand twenty-seven.

howItsDone: The feast of Saint Matthew, apostle and evangelist, is kept on 21 September with its own Mass readings, often including the call at the tax booth from Matthew 9.

fork.setup: you're Matthew. you've just walked away from your tax table to follow Jesus. what do you do first?
options: leave town quietly so no one sees
throw a dinner for your old crowd
go back and close the books properly
fork.reveal: Luke says Levi made a great feast in his house, and Matthew's gospel puts publicans and sinners at that table: the new follower brought his old friends along.

original.note: the Greek gospel word for a tax collector, the old trade the Douay-Rheims renders as publican.

trapdoor: what you thought: one of the twelve, a name on the first gospel.
what it means: a man in a despised job who got up when called and brought his friends to dinner.
what a scholar hears: Mark and Luke call him Levi; in Matthew 10:3 the list of the twelve adds the label the publican to his name.

notes: Confirm exact Challoner wording of Matthew 9:9 ('And he arose up and followed him'), 9:12 and 9:13.
'The Church has long read Levi and Matthew as one person': confirm phrasing; some scholars question the identification.
Authorship stated as Catholic tradition, not as historical fact; Keeper to confirm wording.
Trapdoor: Matthew 10:3 is the only list of the twelve that adds 'the publican'; confirm against Mark 3 and Luke 6.
Peter returning to his boats refers to John 21:3; confirm the aside is fair.
The onlookers in 9:11 are Pharisees in the text; the script says 'some onlookers' to avoid making them the foil.
